title: Primality testing: trial division vs AKS
problem_statement: Given an integer N >= 0, decide whether N is prime.

input.size_measure: n bits (the standard binary encoding of N).

algorithms.name: trial division
algorithms.idea: Try every odd divisor d with d^2 <= N.
algorithms.pseudocode: if N < 2: no; if N even: N == 2; for d = 3, 5, 7, ... while d*d <= N: if d | N: no; yes
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(sqrt(N)) = Theta(2^(n/2)) divisions in the worst case (N prime)
algorithms.correctness: A composite N has a divisor d with 1 < d <= sqrt(N).

algorithms.name: AKS
algorithms.idea: N is prime iff (X + a)^N = X^N + a mod (X^r - 1, N) for a small r and few a, after ruling out perfect powers and small factors. Working modulo X^r - 1 keeps polynomials of degree < r = O(n^5).
algorithms.pseudocode: see implementation (the six steps of AKS 2004, Section 4)
algorithms.time_complexity: Õ(n^(21/2)) as proven in AKS 2004 (Õ(n^(15/2)) using Fouvry's theorem); Õ(n^6) for the Lenstra-Pomerance variant
algorithms.space_complexity: Õ(n^6) bits in the original analysis (r coefficients of n bits each, r = O(n^5))
algorithms.correctness: Agrawal, Kayal, Saxena 2004, Theorem 4.1 (the algorithm returns PRIME iff N is prime).

relationship: Trial division is exponential in the input size n (2^(n/2)); AKS is polynomial in n. Same problem, same deterministic model: the first unconditional deterministic polynomial-time primality test.

sources.authors: Agrawal, M.; Kayal, N.; Saxena, N.
sources.title: PRIMES is in P

sources.authors: Lenstra, H. W., Jr.; Pomerance, C.
sources.title: Primality testing with Gaussian periods
sources.venue: Journal of the European Mathematical Society 21(4), 1229-1269

verification.method: Both implementations agree with each other and with a sieve-of-Eratosthenes oracle on random n-bit integers (half of them primes), n = 0..20 (AKS up to 16 bits, where step 5 is genuinely exercised: N > r). Trial division's 2^(n/2) scaling is measured; AKS scaling is not (its polynomial only dominates far beyond what pure Python can time), so the pair stays at V1.

caveats: AKS matters for theory. In practice primality is tested with Miller-Rabin/BPSW (probabilistic) or ECPP (certificate-producing). 'Exponential' for trial division refers to the bit length n. Trial division is polynomial in the value N, which is exponentially larger than the input.
notes: See primality-miller-rabin-vs-aks for the randomized-vs-deterministic (T4) view of the same problem.
